items.title: Makkah Agreement
items.description: THE Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye on Aug 7, stands out for one clause: an attack on any of the three countries is an attack on all. Coming in the wake of the recent tensions in the Middle East, this agreement has the potential to reshape the strategic layout of the region. Pakistan’s foreign ministry has described the agreement as a reflection of a “shared commitment” to further strengthen the “collective security” of the region. Understandably, the Makkah Agreement does not give the specifics of the commitments that each side has made. Such matters lie in the realm of operational details that are generally kept confidential. What is, however, clear is that it is not a military bloc. Nor is it aimed at any specific country. Since these three countries have different threat perceptions, the agreement seems to be an attempt to enhance their collective deterrence and defence capabilities to deal with any aggression. In the midst of the US-Iran tensions, Saudi Arabia came to the conclusion that the American security umbrella was not working. It started exploring multilayered security arrangements, including a strategic mutual defence agreement with Pakistan and a civil nuclear agreement with the US. In some ways, the Makkah Agreement is an upgrade on the existing Pak-Saudi defence agreement. Anchored in Turkiye’s defence manufacturing capabilities, Saudi Arabia’s financial heft and Pakistan’s trained forces and capabilities, as demonstrated in the war with India in May 2025 , the agreement marks an important strategic landmark in the evolution of a new security architecture of West Asia. Beyond the three countries’ deterrence and defence needs, there are regional and global aspects to discuss. Detractors are projecting it as an anti-Iran, Sunni group. The Turkish foreign minister has stated clearly that neither Iran nor anyone else was the target of this agreement. Iran’s spokesperson also indicated that Iran has no reason to fear the agreement, as regional countries, rather than outside powers, were working on regional security. Importantly, the Makkah Agreement ensures that there would be no single regional hegemon should America decide to retreat from the area. Given that the agreement is predicated on the idea of collective security, Iran and other countries in the neighbourhood could possibly join the agreement in due course so that a durable regional security architecture is established. The accord shouldn’t be seen as a military bloc. The Makkah Agreement is also a strong signal to Israel that its ambition of establishing Greater Israel and dominating the region is over. The US strategy to use the Abraham Accords to integrate Israel into Gulf security is also no longer plausible. The three signatories have consistently called upon Israel to stop its genocide of Palestinians in Gaza and respect international law and UN resolutions calling for an independent state of Palestine based on the pre-1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital. The accord reduces the US burden of protecting the Gulf states and places the region on the path of self-reliance through collective security. America has two vested interests in the region. One is Israel’s security. The second is the continuity of petro-dollars. The US-Iran war has shown the limits of Israeli regional dominance, while America will do its utmost to ensure that the pricing of oil remains in US dollars. The petro-dollar is increasingly likely to be challenged by several countries desiring to buy Iranian and other oil in non-dollar currencies. Yet, it is important for the three signatories to take the US on boa­rd on the scope of this agreement. As for China, it will be pleased with the ag­­reement as it helps expand its concept of collective security encapsulated in the Global Security Initiative. As it is, any step that seems to weaken America’s footprint in the region is a welcome development in Chinese and Russian eyes. Pakistan’s leadership has done well by consistently using its peace diplomacy to not only bring stability to the region but also shape an entirely new image of the country. At the same time, Pakistan must continue its constructive engagement with Iran and major powers. While these strategic alignments serve the interests of the three signatories and the region, it would be useful to explore a corresponding initiative of concluding a trilateral economic agreement to pool together resources for the shared interests of the three states. The ultimate message of the Makkah Agreement is that the region is secure only when every country located in it is safe and when a culture of cooperation replaces one of confrontation. It is also clear that diplomacy backed by credible defence capabilities is the best guard against kinetic misadventures. The writer is former foreign secretary and chairman of Sanober Institute. Published in Dawn, August 16th, 2026

items.title: Saonré : Les populations saluent la construction d’un complexe scolaire et plaident pour un centre de santé
items.description: Les populations de Saonré, à Ouagadougou, se sont mobilisées dans la matinée du samedi 15 août 2026 pour exprimer leur gratitude au chef de l’État, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, et à son gouvernement pour les différentes réalisations engagées dans leur localité, notamment la construction d’un complexe scolaire moderne. À cette occasion, elles ont également formulé un nouveau plaidoyer en faveur de la construction d’un centre de santé de proximité. Ils étaient plusieurs centaines à s’être rassemblés à Saonré pour « dire merci » au chef de l’État pour avoir donné une suite favorable à leurs sollicitations. Selon les habitants, la localité était confrontée à un déficit important d’infrastructures scolaires, contraignant les enfants à parcourir plusieurs kilomètres pour rejoindre les établissements situés notamment à Pissy ou à Cissin. Cette situation appartient désormais au passé, puisque le gouvernement a achevé courant cette année, la construction d’un complexe scolaire moderne au profit de la population. Le chef de Saonré a remercié les autorités burkinabè pour cette infrastructure éducative Pour le chef de Saonré, cette infrastructure constitue un véritable soulagement pour les habitants, qui pourront désormais scolariser leurs enfants dans un établissement public situé à proximité. «Nous disons merci au Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré pour cette école ultramoderne qu’il met à la disposition de notre village. C’était une réelle préoccupation pour nous. Nos enfants devaient parcourir des kilomètres et braver tous les dangers pour rejoindre leurs écoles. Aujourd’hui, c’est du passé et nous ne pouvons que dire merci », a-t-il déclaré.» Le chef de Saonré a, par ailleurs, appelé la population à soutenir les initiatives du gouvernement visant à améliorer les conditions de vie des communautés. Il a particulièrement salué l’engagement de la Veille citoyenne de Bonheur Ville, qu’il a présentée comme ayant joué un rôle important dans la concrétisation de cette réalisation. Une vue de l'école Un plaidoyer citoyen à l’origine du projet Prenant la parole, Daouda Ouédraogo, président du Comité de Veille Citoyenne de Bonheur Ville (CVC-BV), a souligné que la construction du complexe scolaire est l’aboutissement d’un processus de plaidoyer, de concertation et de mobilisation ayant impliqué plusieurs acteurs. Selon lui, cette réalisation illustre la capacité d’une mobilisation citoyenne responsable, menée dans le respect des autorités et des procédures administratives, à contribuer à la résolution concrète des préoccupations des populations. « La population de Bonheur Ville avait, à travers le Comité de veille citoyenne, identifié plusieurs priorités d’ordre vital pour notre secteur. Parmi ces priorités figurait la nécessité de disposer d’une infrastructure scolaire adaptée aux besoins de la population. Nos enfants parcouraient plusieurs kilomètres avant de rejoindre leurs écoles à Pissy ou à Cissin. Aujourd’hui, cette question est résolue », a-t-il expliqué tout en exprimant sa reconnaissance aux autorités burkinabè, avec à leur tête le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, pour la réalisation de l’infrastructure. Daouda Ouédraogo, président du Comité de Veille Citoyenne de Bonheur Ville (CVC-BV) « Sans l’avènement du Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, cette réalisation n’aurait pas eu lieu. Donc, nous disons merci à notre président. Et selon ce qui ressort des propos du ministre de l'enseignement de base, les établissements scolaires du Burkina Faso seront désormais construits suivant ce modèle », a-t-il ajouté. Après l’école, le centre de santé Tout en saluant la réalisation du complexe scolaire, les populations de Saonré ont formulé un nouveau plaidoyer : la construction d’une infrastructure sanitaire dans la zone. A en croire Daouda Ouédraogo, le village ne dispose actuellement d’aucune infrastructure sanitaire publique, une situation qui constitue un obstacle important à l’accès aux soins. Les populations ont traduit leur gratitude au Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré « Si l’accès à l’éducation connaît une avancée importante, l’accès aux soins de santé demeure une préoccupation majeure. La croissance démographique et l’extension de la zone rendent indispensable la mise en place d’une infrastructure sanitaire de proximité », a-t-il relevé.» Pour le président du CVC-BV, la construction d’un centre de santé permettrait notamment de rapprocher les soins des populations, de réduire les distances parcourues pour accéder aux services sanitaires, d’améliorer la prise en charge des femmes enceintes et des enfants, de faciliter les consultations et les soins de première nécessité, mais aussi de renforcer la prévention et la sensibilisation en matière de santé. « Le centre de santé n’est donc pas un luxe. Il constitue aujourd’hui une nécessité sociale et sanitaire », a-t-il insisté. Des démarches engagées depuis 2024 Conscientes de cette nécessité, les populations, sous la houlette du CVC-BV, indiquent avoir engagé, dès janvier 2024, des démarches auprès du ministère chargé de la Santé. Le principe du projet aurait reçu un avis favorable, avant que le Comité ne soit orienté vers les services techniques compétents. Une vue des femmes à cette assemblée Le CVC-BV a ainsi été mis en relation avec le directeur régional de la Santé, qui a, à son tour, instruit le District sanitaire de Pissy afin qu’une visite du site destiné à accueillir l’infrastructure soit effectuée. Cette visite technique a effectivement eu lieu et a permis aux services compétents de prendre connaissance de la situation ainsi que du site envisagé pour l’implantation du futur centre de santé. À ce jour, selon les populations, malgré les différentes démarches entreprises et les avis favorables enregistrés au cours du processus, le Comité reste dans l’attente de l’autorisation nécessaire à l’exploitation du site destiné à accueillir l’infrastructure sanitaire. Lire aussi : Ouagadougou : Des habitants de Bonheur-ville s’insurgent contre « l’attribution » de leur réserve à une opératrice économique « Cette autorisation constitue désormais une étape déterminante pour permettre au projet de franchir un nouveau cap et d’entrer dans une phase plus concrète de réalisation » , a souligné Daouda Ouédraogo. Le président du CVC-BV a ainsi invité les autorités concernées à donner suite à cette démarche, au regard de l’importance du projet pour les populations de Saonré, qui, du reste, se disent mobilisées et prêtes à prendre en charge dès obtention de l'autorisation, la construction de la clôture du site devant abriter l'infrastructure. Oumarou KONATE Minute.bf

items.title: Osun election: Adeleke leads Oyebamiji
items.description: · Vote sold for N30, 000 as violence mars poll ·Aregbesola loses PU to Oyebamiji By Dayo Johnson, Dapo Akinrefon & Shina Abubakar Governor Ademola Adeleke of the Accord Party jumped into early lead over his All Progressives Congress, APC, challenger, Mr Bola Oyebamiji, in the tightly contested Osun State governorship election, last night. With results from 3,292 polling units or 87.5 percent of the 3,763 polling units uploaded by the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, as of press time, Adeleke had garnered over 439,132 votes compared to Oyebamiji’s 379,255 votes. Read: Osun Election Live Updates: INEC begins collation announcement of results The poll recorded impressive voter turnout but was marred by vote-buying and violence. Despite assurances of a violence-free exercise, there were pockets of violence recorded in some areas across the state. Adeleke sweeps polling unit Adeleke won his polling unit at Ward 02, PU 009, Abogunde Compound, Ede North LGA, by polling 421 votes. The announcement sparked jubilation among supporters who gathered at the unit. Earlier in the day, Adeleke voted at Sagba Abogunde Ward 2, Unit 9, and said he was confident of victory. Omisore loses polling unit Adeleke equally won the polling unit of former Osun Deputy Governor, Senator Iyiola Omisore, who, a few days before the election, declared his support for Oyebamiji Results on the INEC Result Viewing Portal, IReV, showed that Accord polled 131 votes at PU 003, Ife Ward 1, Moore, St. Gabriel Primary School, Ife East LGA. The APC finished second with 85 votes, while ADC got 10 votes. Other parties recorded marginal votes. Gov defeats Oyinlola at polling unity Earlier, the governor won at the polling unit of former Governor Olagunsoye Oyinlola in Okuku, Odo-Otin LGA, with 125 votes. APC got 85 votes, ADC 5. Oyinlola publicly declared his support for APC’s Oyebamiji after a spat with the governor. Oyebamiji wins Aregbesola’s polling unit However, the APC’s Oyebamiji recorded a landslide win at the polling unit of former Osun Governor, Ogbeni Rauf Aregbesola, in Ilesa. Results from the unit showed APC polling 256 votes to defeat Adeleke, who scored 43 votes. Aregbesola, the African Democratic Congress, ADC, National Secretary, worked for Dr Najeem Salaam, the party’s standard-bearer, who finished third with 13 votes. The former governor, a major political figure in Ijesaland, voted at the unit earlier in the day amid heavy presence of voters and observers. ICC raises alarm over plan to declare poll inconclusive Meanwhile, the Imole Campaign Council, ICC, yesterday, alleged that there was a plot by lNEC to declare the election inconclusive. Chairman of its Media and Publicity, Bamidele Salam, said the move was being pushed by APC governors and leaders to frustrate the “imminent victory” of Senator Adeleke of the Accord Party. Salam, in a statement, said: “Our party wishes to inform Nigerians of a sinister plan by INEC to declare the ongoing governorship election inconclusive, to hijack our candidate’s victory and subvert the will of the gallant Osun electorate.” He urged INEC Chairman to honour his pledge of a free, fair and credible poll, and reminded INEC, APC and security agencies of President Bola Tinubu’s directive that the election should not be compromised. Salam also called on the ‘’IGP, DSS DG, and NSCDC Commandant-General to provide security at all collation centres to stop “hoodlums hired by the APC.” He cited reports of ballot box snatching in some polling units and demanded arrests. Salam further called on local and international observers to speak out “on the side of the law and people of Osun State.” Political parties engage in vote-buying Meanwhile, agents of the frontline parties were seen engaging in vote-buying. At AUD Primary School in Atile, Ikire, Irewole LGA, Sunday Vanguard observed that party agents stationed themselves around polling booths to monitor the voters. The move, it was observed, was to monitor voters and their ballot papers to ensure they cast their votes for their candidate. It was further observed that as soon as a voter casts his or her vote, a party agent hands over a tag to enable the voter claim his or her cash. An Accord Party agent, Ajayi Ayodele, was seen accusing APC agents of clustering around the polling booths to monitor the ballot papers. Agents of the APC made similar allegations against Accord Party. Security agents were unable to curb the activities of the party agents. A security agent, names withheld, lamented that he had tried to prevent the agents from loitering around the polling booths but his efforts proved abortive. It was further gathered that political parties offered between N30,000 and N20,000 to induce voters. ICPC monitors polling units As a way of preventing inducement of voters, the operatives of the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission, ICPC, were on the ground in Ejigbo. The officials of the anti-graft agency monitored activities in several polling units across the local government headquarters, including Unit 009, Ward 001; Unit 005, Ward 003; and Unit 006 and Ward 004. At the units visited, ICPC operatives observed the conduct of voters and party agents, and inspected activities around the polling centres. Their presence attracted attention, with some voters pausing to watch as the officials carried out monitoring duties. Civil society flays vote- buying Submitting its report on the election, the Co-Convener of the Nigeria Civil Society Situation Room, Celestine Odo, said there were reports of vote-buying and electoral inducement. He said: “There were observations of vote-buying and all forms of electoral inducement, including sharing of Jollof Rice and drinks in PU008, Ward 6 Isokan LGA, which caused a lot of disorderliness. The credibility of an election is fundamentally undermined when voters are pressured or induced to exchange their votes for money, gifts or other benefits. Political actors must respect the freedom of voters to make their choices without coercion.” Police arrest lawmaker Before the exercise took off, Osun State Police Command arrested a serving member of the State House of Assembly, Mr Ibrahim Inaolaji, alongside 143 suspected electoral mercenaries camped at his residence in Ikire. The lawmaker, who represents Irewole/Isokan State Constituency in the Osun State House of Assembly, was arrested on Friday night during an operation. More than 200 Permanent Voter Cards, PVCs, were reportedly recovered during the operation. In a video clip, Ibrahim was seen making a preliminary statement where he identified himself and allegedly confessed to facilitating the movement of the 146 suspects into Osun State from neighbouring states. According to the police, preliminary investigations indicated that the suspects were brought into Osun from Ondo State to participate in unlawful electoral activities. The suspects reportedly told investigators that they were recruited by a yet-to-be-identified politician, who allegedly facilitated the procurement of voters’ cards for them and instructed them to vote in exchange for financial rewards. The Command’s spokesperson, Abiodun Ojelabi, said investigations had commenced to identify and apprehend other accomplices still at large and to unravel the full extent of the alleged network involved in the recruitment of electoral mercenaries, voter inducement and other related offences. ADC candidate, Salaam escapes assassination The exercise took a dangerous turn as ADC governorship candidate, Mr Najeem Salaam, reportedly escaped assassination in Ejigbo area of the state. Salaam, according to the party’s Publicity Secretary in the state, Abosede Oluwaseun, escaped an alleged assassination attempt at Ward 4, Unit 13, in Ejigbo Local Government Area, shortly after casting his vote. Oluwaseun said the party’s candidate “was swiftly whisked away by concerned locals who acted quickly to prevent the situation from escalating. “Had it not been for the timely intervention and intelligence of residents at the scene, what happened could have resulted in yet another tragic loss of life.” He said the incident disrupted voting and was accompanied by alleged electoral irregularities, raising serious concerns about the integrity of the voting process in the affected area. “This is unacceptable. Democracy must never become a battlefield, and no Nigerian should have to risk their life simply for exercising their constitutional right to vote. “We call on security agencies and relevant authorities to immediately investigate this incident, identify those responsible, and ensure the safety of all voters, party agents and candidates. “Dr. Najeem Salaam is alive. He remains resolute in his bid to rescue Osun from the shackles of bad governance.” I’m confident of winning – Salaam Despite the assassination attempt on his life, Salaam said he is confident of victory if the election is conducted freely and fairly. He said the people of Osun were “behind his candidacy and eager for change.” The former Speaker of the House of Assembly, said: “Without manipulation, I will win this election. The people of Osun are behind me, and they are ready for change. “What we have been hearing from across the state shows that there is a strong desire for a new direction.” Journalists escape death in Ejigbo Similarly, journalists, who monitored the exercise in Ejigbo, were not spared as hoodlums attacked their vehicles, smashing vehicle windscreens and side screens. Some of the reporters escaped being lynched as suspected hoodlums went haywire, forcing electoral officials to stop the voting process at the unit. Adeleke condemns arrest of Osun PDP chair, demands release Frowning at what he described as “sheer abuse of law enforcement” to intimidate supporters, Governor Ademola condemned the arrest of the Peoples Democratic Party, PDP, chairman in the state, Mr Sunday Bisi, in his home after he had voted. The governor described it as barbaric and a vicious attack on free will. The governor, in a statement issued by his spokesperson, Olawale Rasheed, disclosed that the PDP chairman was arrested at his home shortly after casting his vote. Adeleke said: “Information reaching me indicates that Mr Bisi was accosted in his home in Ilesa shortly after he returned after voting, and whisked him away to a yet-to-be-known location. Up until this moment, no one has provided the reason for his arrest, which indicates that the APC is working in cohort with compromised security agents to keep people away from monitoring results at the various collation centres. “This latest sweep on my supporters, I have authoritatively learned, is part of a broader plan to give the APC unhindered access to change results at collation centres and upturn our wins at the poll. “This is the biggest assault on democracy, and I urge everyone involved in this desperate attempt to upturn the will of our people through the use of state institutions. “In that regard, I am calling for the immediate release of Mr Bisi because his arrest is nothing but political and other political prisoners across Osun State. Elections should be about the people freely giving their mandates to the person of their choice without threat or force.” Adewusi, Adereti’s supporters clash in Ife There was a brief disruption at the polling unit of Osun State Deputy Governor and Accord Party’s deputy governorship candidate, Prince Kola Adewusi, in Ile-Ife, after a confrontation broke out between supporters. The incident occurred when APC deputy governorship candidate, Benjamin Kayode Adereti, arrived at the polling unit. Both party leaders are from Ile-Ife. Adereti had earlier voted at his designated polling unit, Waasin Polling Unit 11, Ilaare Ward 3, before proceeding to Adewusi’s polling location. It was gathered that his presence was challenged by some supporters of Adewusi who were already at the unit, leading to heated exchanges and raised tensions. The confrontation briefly disrupted the peaceful atmosphere at the polling unit before calm was restored. The reason for Adereti’s visit to the deputy governor’s polling unit could not be confirmed as of the time of filing this report. Adeleke’s camp accuses security agents of intimidation The Imole Campaign Council, ICC, yesterday, accused the Nigerian Army and other security agencies of partisanship and intimidation in Osun State, warning that the military must not be used as “pawns in the hands of desperate power-seeking politicians.” The ICC, in a statement by its spokesperson, Mr Pelumi Olajengbesi, alleged that soldiers stormed the homes of Accord Party leaders across the state, especially in Osun East Senatorial District, and arrested key party members on election day. He said: “Over 15 trucks of soldiers raided residences on Friday night and detained innocent individuals. “This development is shocking and undemocratic. Innocent citizens should not be picked up on election day.” EU observers report vote trading, BVAS glitches The EU Support to Democratic Governance in Nigeria Election Observation Hub, EU-SDGN EOH, reported 323 cases of electoral offences and 38 security incidents during the exercise. In its preliminary statement, the Hub said the figures were based on reports from 823 accredited observers deployed across the 30 LGAs of the state. The Hub comprises CEMESO, IPC, NWTF, TAF Africa, The Kukah Centre and Yiaga Africa. The Hub said 2,339,233 voters were registered, with 1,906,390, or 81.5%, collecting PVCs. Of the 726 polling units observed, officials with complete materials arrived in 608 units, 83.7%, between 7:30am and 8am. Another 75 units got materials between 8am-8:30am, and 42 units between 8:30am-11am. One PU had not opened by 11am. 58 BVAS devices, 7.9%, malfunctioned, but 41, 70.7%, were rectified. Turnout was described as “impressive” and voting was largely peaceful and orderly. The 323 infractions, it stated, included “103 cases of vote trading, 85 cases of exposed ballots, 38 cases of campaigning at PUs, 31 cases of voter obstruction, 28 cases of inducement of officials, 14 cases of impersonation, 12 cases of multiple voting and 7 cases of official misconduct.” Security incidents recorded included thuggery, attacks on officials and voter intimidation. Specific cases were cited at PU 29-10-10-005, Igbon DC School, Ejigbo and PU 29-26-01-002 & PU 29-30-06-015, Okanla Area, Osogbo. Octogenarian casts ballot, charges young voters On the sidelines, age was no barrier for Chief Ramon Busari, the Oluode of Ejigbo, as he joined other voters at Unit 04, Ward 1 to cast his ballot during the exercise. The 80-year-old traditional title holder was seen patiently waiting on the queue, saying voting remains both a right and a responsibility. Busari, who said: “I still feel obliged to help choose leaders for our state,’’ used the opportunity to charge young people to come out and vote. He said: “Your votes matter. Do not stay away from the polls. Participate peacefully and decide the future you want.” According to him, abstaining from elections cedes power to others. Don’t give up on elections, 97-year-old voter urges Nigerians Also, a 97-year-old great grandfather, Pa Isaac Adeniran Adesanmi, yesterday, said he would always vote during any election because it is his civic right. The elder statesman is one of the elderly who joined the electorate at NUD Primary School, Collation Centre, Unit 1, Ward 4, Ilase Ijesa in Obokun Local Government Area to cast their votes. Adesanmi was brought to the polling unit by his relatives to exercise his franchise. However, Pa Adesanmi could not be accredited on time as the BVAs could not capture his face and fingerprint. INEC officials urged him to be patient and promised to try it again. In an interview, Pa Adesanmi, whose number on the voters list is 116, said he had not stopped voting since he started during the days of the late Obafemi Awolowo. “I am 97 years old, and I started voting during the time of Awolowo. “I always vote anytime an election comes up. I have been voting in Kaduna before I came back home,” he said. On his advice for the youths and other Nigerians, he said: “I will advise youths to vote because if they do not, the type of leaders they want will not be there. My message to Nigerians is to continue to vote at all costs and vote for the people they like.” Asked to advise the potential winner after the voting exercise, the nonagenarian said: “I want them to do as they promise.” The post Osun election: Adeleke leads Oyebamiji appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Balochistan’s wounds
items.description: ALTHOUGH Balochistan has been experiencing varying degrees of tumult for over two decades now, currently, the troubled province is witnessing near-constant terrorist activity and lawlessness. The rulers in both Islamabad and Quetta often downplay the situation, but there are moments when they themselves admit that all is not well in Balochistan. For instance, on Friday, when the nation was celebrating Independence Day, the province’s Chief Minister Sarfraz Bugti extended an olive branch to those engaged in violence. Mr Bugti advised the lawless elements to “return to the national mainstream” and talk to the government. However, he added, and rightly so, that the state would not talk to those who were involved in the killing of innocent people. In recent times, terrorist activity in Balochistan has become noticeably brazen. While ordinary citizens and security personnel are often targeted, even the high-level guardians of the state are not safe. On Friday, Balochistan Home Minister Ziaullah Langove’s convoy came under attack as he was returning to Quetta from Kalat. The minister survived the ambush, but a number of personnel who were accompanying him were wounded in the attack. Elsewhere, security forces have not yet given clearance for repair work on a gas pipeline that was blown up by the terrorists. The latter’s act of sabotage has deprived several towns of gas. While the chief minister has once again invited ‘angry’ elements for talks, the state has yet to create conducive conditions for dialogue to get off the ground. At this point, some introspection is required: the state has alienated even those political elements in Baloch society that have been peacefully pursuing their rights. This attitude must change. In the short term, a genuine process of reconciliation can begin by inviting both veteran Baloch politicians and younger activists to the table, and listening to their grievances. Questionable cases against peaceful activists should also be reviewed. If the state is able to build confidence through such measures, the next step can be taken to address long-term goals, such as ensuring that the people of Balochistan are given the first right to their province’s vast mineral wealth. The province’s miserable socioeconomic numbers also need the state’s immediate attention; this may take decades to fix, but the first step must be taken now. Claims that hostile foreign forces are stirring up trouble in Balochistan carry much weight. These forces must be exposed and kinetic action should continue against those involved in terrorism in Balochistan. But a long-term solution lies in taking the political path and involving the genuine representatives of the residents. The people will be waiting to see what practical steps the state takes to take forward the process of reconciliation in the province. Published in Dawn, August 16th, 2026

items.title: Inside Lagos’ waste, flood crisis (2): LAWMA, refuse collectors shift blame
items.description: By Olasunkanmi Akoni, Esther Onyegbula, Juliet Umeh & Cynthia Alo In the first part of this report published last Sunday, Lagos residents and council chairmen traded claims on refuse heaps ‘decorating’ roads in the state. Today, the regulator of waste, Lagos Waste Management Authority (LAWMA), and refuse collectors under the aegis of PSP Operators share their perspectives. Read on. Addressing the issue of waste on roads’ median in Lagos, Managing Director of Lagos Waste Management Authority, LAWMA, Dr. Muyiwa Gbadegesin, stressed that keeping the state clean remains a collective responsibility. According to him, the problem of refuse in Lagos has persisted because some residents have decided that they will put their waste on the road instead of giving it to PSP operators. He said: “Lagos will be free from dirt when Lagosians decide that Lagos will be free from dirt. It is collective. If everyone in Lagos decides today that there is not going to be waste on the road again, then we won’t have a problem. “But now, some people have decided that they will put their waste on the road instead of giving it to the PSP operator. “If you have any delay in your collection, reach out to LAWMA. Don’t bring your waste to the roadside. That’s when we will stop having waste on the roadside”. Gbadegesin, however, assured that the heaps of refuse across the state will soon be a thing of the past following strategic intervention aimed at strengthening waste evacuation operations and improving waste management infrastructure. The LAWMA MD spoke during the commissioning of the rehabilitated Road E and newly constructed disposal platforms at the Olusosun Disposal Facility, Ojota. He described the project as another significant milestone in the Lagos State Government’s efforts to eliminate operational bottlenecks, improve access within the disposal facility and enhance the efficiency of waste evacuation across the state. Municipal According to him, the rehabilitation of Road E became necessary after recent heavy rainfall affected access to parts of the facility, slowing the movement of compactor trucks responsible for evacuating municipal waste from different parts of the state. The upgraded access road, he said, would improve access for waste evacuation vehicles, enable more trucks to discharge simultaneously and reduce turnaround time at one of the state’s busiest waste disposal facilities. Gbadegesin said: “We announced that the site, we’re winding down activities, and that we have a timeline. “If you recall, we said 18 months from the time that we did groundbreaking on construction of the transfer loading station. “You have been seeing trucks coming and going and you have also been seeing the queues. “What we’ve done here is to reclaim a portion so that we can have somewhere to dispose as we wind down the activity. “That’s what we’ve achieved, and some of the waste backlog on the roads will be cleared away because it is not a good thing for us to have waste on our roads. “By opening this place, we have created more space. Over the next few days there won’t be refuse on our roads. ”This project represents another important milestone in our commitment to building a more efficient and resilient waste management system for Lagos. By improving access to the disposal facility and expanding operational capacity, we are addressing immediate challenges while laying the foundation for long term improvements in waste evacuation across the state.” Olusosun Gbadegesin noted that the intervention reflected Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu’s commitment to strengthening critical waste management infrastructure through strategic collaboration with the private sector. He commended Zoomlion Nigeria Limited for rehabilitating the road, saying the company’s support had evolved beyond Corporate Social Responsibility into a broader technical collaboration in waste infrastructure development. “Waste management is highly resource intensive, and addressing the challenges requires strategic partnerships, technical expertise and sustained investment. We are pleased that our collaboration with Zoomlion is contributing to the transformation of critical waste management infrastructure in Lagos,” he stated. The LAWMA boss disclosed that Zoomlion is currently constructing modern Transfer Loading Stations at Olusosun and Solous III, each designed to process 2,500 metric tonnes of waste daily. He added that the state government is also implementing other long term infrastructure projects, including Material Recovery Facilities, waste to energy plants, biogas facilities and the planned acquisition of additional compactor trucks over the next three years. Gbadegesin said Olusosun currently handles about half of the municipal solid waste generated daily in Lagos, making continuous investment in waste infrastructure indispensable as the state gradually transitions to a more integrated and environmentally sustainable waste management system. While reaffirming LAWMA’s commitment to improving waste management services, he urged residents to patronise assigned PSP operators, pay promptly for waste collection services and refrain from indiscriminate dumping of refuse. Managing Director of Zoomlion Nigeria Limited, Mrs. Habiba Abubakar, disclosed that the project was completed within 26 days, ahead of schedule, describing the rehabilitated road and disposal platforms as the first phase of a broader partnership with LAWMA. PSP Operators react Speaking on the waste management challenge in the state, the National President of the Association of Waste Managers of Nigeria, AWAMN, Mr. Oluwagbenga Adebola, said Lagos is facing infrastructure deficit in the area that will support effective and efficient waste collection, transportation, and disposal. According to him, this inhibits quick turnaround time for compactor trucks. He also spoke of people doing indiscriminate dumping, people who don’t want to patronize PSP operators, and people not wanting to pay for services rendered Adebola said: “For the drivers and all the crew operating on the trucks, some of them spend several days here, and it impacts negatively on their wellbeing and their health. “You can imagine a driver and evacuator staying here for several days. This is a mosquito infested area. “Mosquitoes bite them, they suffer malaria and other illnesses. When you stay too long here, you are exposed to all manners of health challenges. Generally, I think it is going to improve their wellbeing.” He added that operators also incur heavy financial losses whenever trucks remain stranded at the dumpsite. “As operators and business owners, we are more or less at the receiving end. Every truck that sleeps here comes with consequences. “People tamper with the trucks, damage them and even steal diesel. “Before now, bulldozers had to push trucks in and out because of the bad roads and that also affected the vehicles. “All these are likely going to stop.” He described the rehabilitation of the Olusosun access road as unprecedented. “I will say it is unprecedented. It is a big kudos to Zoomlion, LAWMA and the Lagos State Government,” he said. Adebola expressed optimism that ongoing investments in Transfer Loading Stations and other waste management infrastructure would further strengthen the state’s environmental management system and support LAWMA’s long term reform agenda. “It will bring about quick turnaround time of the trucks. Once the trucks are able to dump within a very short period, it will definitely improve the overall service delivery of waste collection, transportation and disposal in Lagos State. “We will have a cleaner, healthier and more aesthetic Lagos.” He added that the intervention would serve as a stopgap while the transfer loading stations are being completed. “Almost over 50 per cent of the waste collection in Lagos patronises Olusosun. So, if Olusosun sneezes, every Lagosian will catch cold. It is a good development for us and I hope it will be sustained.” Adebola also said the rehabilitation would ease the persistent traffic congestion around the Olusosun axis. “Even the traffic around this axis will be impacted positively. Before now, accessing this place was a terrible experience because of the long queues. Once we achieve a turnaround time of one hour or less, that traffic will disappear.” 20 trucks Adebola said reduced waiting time would enable operators to increase the number of daily evacuation trips and improve service delivery across Lagos. “Before now, trucks could only make two or three trips daily. Now we should be able to have nothing less than eight trucks dumping simultaneously. “With additional facilities, that could increase to between 16 and 20 trucks. That is going to impact positively on almost everything.” He added: “Road E has been completed so that waste collection trucks coming from households can drive in smoothly, dump their waste quickly and return to collect more refuse from house to house and neighbourhood to neighbourhood. “When waste is collected efficiently and dumped without delays, the environment stays clean.” Dumpsites Adebola urged residents to support government and PSP operators by disposing waste responsibly. His words: “The key takeaway is that this project will help prevent indiscriminate waste dumping across Lagos State. “We appeal to citizens not to dump waste everywhere but to wait for the collectors. “Right now, this site has given us some relief and we hope other dumpsites will also be developed because we have about five major disposal sites. “If people put their waste out properly for collection, it will reduce diseases like malaria. Waste is not really waste unless you make it so. “Waste is actually a valuable resource. If processed properly, there is money in it. “Our advice is that everyone should cooperate because a single hand cannot lift a heavy load onto the head.” PSPs’ challenges On the challenges faced by PSP operators, Adebola said: “I think we cannot overemphasize this issue. We are currently facing a challenge that is very, very unfortunate. “Lagos is facing what we call an infrastructure deficit in the area of infrastructure that will support effective and efficient waste collection, transportation, and disposal. “PSPs will collect waste, and that’s the only thing that the residents know. After the PSP collect the waste, people don’t care wherever they go to dump it, wherever they take it to. “However, if where they are going to take it has a challenge, inaccessible roads, dump sites are almost at the point of filled up, you know, of course, occasioned by even the constant, continuous rain in June, July, and all that affected the overall turnaround of the trucks. “The turn-around time of the trucks is affected. “So if the trucks collect waste and they are unable to dump, then there’s no way they can go back and collect the waste, which is the number one challenge that we have. “Of course, there are so many other challenges: Of people doing indiscriminate dumping, people who don’t want to patronize PSP operators, and, you know, people not wanting to pay for services rendered. “Of course, some people might say, the PSPs are having truck challenges. Yes, we have some aging trucks, but it is not that bad. “At the last count, we were having over 100 or close to 1,000 trucks parading the streets of Lagos. Even if you have 2,000 trucks or 3,000 trucks and they are unable to get somewhere to dump their waste, it will all be stranded somewhere. “And what are the measures? We have made it abundantly clear that we have been working with the government. And one of it is the commissioning of the Road E, one of the roads at Olusosun. That has actually brought about the creation of two platforms where PSPs and LAWMA too can dump. “And so, since the commissioning, some few vehicles that have been stranded there for several weeks are now dumping. And then, with time, and hopefully when that place is maintained and sustained, and then there are requisite equipment to really do the day-to-day job, things can improve. “However, it is not only that place that we have a challenge. All the dump sites, disposal sites in Lagos State are challenged: From Olusosun at Ojota to Solous, Igando, Ewu Elepe at Ikorodu, to Gbagada dump site at Badagry, and then to Epe dump site at Epe, all of them do have a major challenge regarding access roads. “Having commissioned Road E, we are hoping—and I know that there is a whole lot of arrangement on ground working with LAWMA and then the state government, in fact, the Ministry of Environment. “We had a meeting yesterday, Thursday, today, Friday, we had a meeting, all for all hands to be on deck to ensure that we have an improvement. “I mean, once the infrastructure that are in deficit are provided, then waste management will go back to the normal effective and efficient service delivery. “There are over 420 PSPs operating in Lagos. And then you’re asking how many of them are operating. I can assure you a large number of these people are operating. “However, there are some challenges where people have actually serviced tenements for several years and then there’s no payment, and then the issue of non-implementation of cost-reflective tariff. “I mean, both the Commissioner for the Environment and Water Resources, and LAWMA have talked about this severally. “The current tariff that is being charged in the industry was set in 2022. That was before the full deregulation of the petroleum sector. “Diesel was just N600 per liter, and diesel went up to N1,500, even up to N2,000 and over N2,000. “The tariff has not changed. That cannot bring sustainability because in waste management, there is what we call the cost element. “If you are not meeting your cost, the cost that you put into the industry, with time, people will just fizzle out. “There are some people that couldn’t even meet up with whatever, and they willingly left the industry because it’s no longer profitable. It’s not a business that they want to stay in. So there are a few of them like that. “However, what we have been appealing and discussing with government, and I believe we are on the same page, is for government to provide an enabling environment: access to the dump sites, implementation of cost-reflective tariffs, and so on and so forth, including enforcement anyway, so that when you invest, you can recoup your money.” The post Inside Lagos’ waste, flood crisis (2): LAWMA, refuse collectors shift blame appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Ceuta al límite: urgencias repletas, vecinos desbordados y ruidos de sirena
items.description: En Ceuta, conocida como la ciudad de las cuatro culturas, hoy caben mil ciudades en una. En el barrio de El Príncipe, a mediodía de este viernes, decenas de niñas y jóvenes migrantes son trasladadas a una nave industrial recién reformada para acogerlas tras acusar la amenaza de violencia sexual. A la misma hora y a pocos kilómetros de allí, en el polígono de El Tarajal , otros tantos menores no acompañados duermen en el suelo entre el hedor a excremento y orín. En una ladera próxima, en la mañana de este sábado, tres legionarios corren con la porra en mano detrás de tres adolescentes y uno les ruega en árabe alejarse de las casas. Poco después, en la playa de El Trampolín, el asentamiento principalmente de subsaharianos ha mutado en poblado donde ya se autoorganizan las tareas y matan su tediosa espera en torneos de lucha libre. Las urgencias del único hospital están colapsadas por la afluencia de personas migrantes, con algunos casos puntuales de tuberculosis y sarna registrados, pero sobre todo debido a heridas por reyertas o caídas. Y la psicosis inunda las mentes y los teléfonos de los ceutíes por las informaciones sobre el aumento de la delincuencia, mientras las sirenas de las patrullas no cesan. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Crimen de Tauste: las 72 horas que llevaron a Carlota y su novio a prisión acusados de matar a los padres de ella
items.description: Carlota actuó de forma extraña desde que se conoció el asesinato de sus padres. Cuando tres familiares acudieron a su vivienda en Zaragoza a darle la noticia, el domingo 9 de agosto, ofreció unas explicaciones confusas sobre por qué no había ido a la comida del día anterior, en la que se supone que iba a coincidir con ellos. Además, llevaba gafas de sol cuando no eran necesarias y se le notaban heridas y golpes en la cara y un brazo. Uno de esos familiares le recomendó ir a urgencias y eso hizo. Al día siguiente, fue detenida junto a su pareja, Luis Carlos Rivera, por su presunta participación en el homicidio de Javier Sánchez, de 67 años, y Esther Latorre, de 66 , un caso que ha supuesto un terremoto entre los que los conocieron y también en el mundo sindical, agrario, político y activista del que formaban parte. El estado mental de Carlota será clave a la hora de dirimir su responsabilidad en el crimen. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El Senado, fuerza de choque institucional
items.description: Wenceslao Fernández Flórez , eminente cronista parlamentario en el final de la Restauración y el comienzo de la República, apenas frecuentaba el Senado. En una ocasión que lo visitó, el escritor coruñés quedó tan sorprendido de la provecta edad de sus señorías que aguzó la cáustica pluma en su sección de Abc : más que una Cámara, escribió, “aquello parece una excavación”. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Los vecinos de Almaraz, sobre alargar la vida de la central nuclear: “No será la última, lucharemos por más”
items.description: Almaraz está de fiesta. Durante la tarde de este sábado, en la plaza del Ayuntamiento, los niños se deslizan por dos toboganes hinchables de unos cuatro metros y saltan en un castillo inflable con forma de jirafa, mientras los adultos comen y beben en una docena de quioscos de cerveza y comida. Shakira y Daddy Yankee suenan alto en los altavoces y una hilera de sacos convertidos en mosaicos, con dibujos de plantas y del escudo municipal, cuelga a la entrada de la plaza. Este fin de semana se celebran las fiestas en honor a San Roque, patrón del municipio y protector frente a todo tipo de pestes, incluida la despoblación que amenaza a este municipio cacereño de 1.594 habitantes. Este año, el pueblo tiene un doble motivo de celebración. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Bruselas se pertrecha ante una posible batalla comercial con China
items.description: La Unión Europea y China han marcado octubre en rojo en sus calendarios. Las negociaciones están en marcha y ese mes Bruselas quiere ver “resultados tangibles” para que empiecen a resolverse los grandes desequilibrios que acumula su relación comercial con el gigante asiático. La desigualdad se observa en un solo dato: la diferencia entre las exportaciones y las importaciones es muy deficitaria, más de 370.000 millones de euros en 2025 y la certeza de que este año, al ritmo que va, todavía será mayor. La Comisión Europea viene diciendo que la negociación y el acuerdo es la prioridad: “Es la oportunidad de reforzar esta relación mediante el compromiso y el diálogo para hacerla más justa y equilibrada”, explica un portavoz. “Pero si el diálogo fracasa, actuaremos”. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Cuando el microcrédito acaba asfixiando la economía familiar: “No podía pagar ni un café”
items.description: Desde que decidió mudarse hace más de 25 años de Ecuador a Olot (Girona), Manuel Carrier, de 51 años, ha querido ser padre. “Quería con quien reír, jugar, disfrutar de la paternidad”, recuerda emocionado. Sin embargo, la vida se lo puso difícil. Él y su mujer gastaron casi 8.000 euros en una clínica privada para un tratamiento de fecundación in vitro, pero cerró y perdieron ese dinero. Lo volvieron a intentar, desembolsaron otros 8.000 euros y finalmente lograron ser padres. Sin embargo, cuenta Carrier, se quedaron a la vez sin ahorros y sin uno de sus principales sustentos económicos: el negocio de repostería que tenían en su país natal quebró. Como el trabajo en España no le daba suficiente para llegar a fin de mes, acudieron a microcréditos, a préstamos de apenas unos cientos de euros. Pero el remedio fue peor que la enfermedad, ya que no pudieron afrontar su devolución con los elevados intereses que comportan. “Llegó un momento en el que no pude pagar ni un café”, relata. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Beyond Surgery: Can nutrition and lifestyle help prevent Uterine Fibroids?
items.description: By Vivian Obi For many Nigerian women, the word fibroid carries more fear than hope. It is a diagnosis often whispered among friends, discussed quietly within families, or discovered unexpectedly after years of enduring painful menstrual periods, heavy bleeding, persistent pelvic pain, or difficulty conceiving. By the time many women seek medical attention, surgery has become the only option presented to them. Across Nigeria, stories of women postponing weddings, delaying pregnancy, struggling with infertility, or travelling long distances in search of treatment have become increasingly common. Families organise fundraisers for surgery. Religious gatherings hold special prayers for women hoping to conceive after a myomectomy. Some women live with symptoms for years because they believe the pain is “normal,” while others avoid hospitals out of fear that they will be told their womb must be removed. These stories are not isolated experiences. They represent a growing public health concern that deserves far more attention than it currently receives. Yet, amid the conversations about surgery and fertility, an equally important question is often overlooked: Can some cases of uterine fibroids be prevented—or at least delayed—through healthier nutrition and lifestyle choices? Recent scientific evidence suggests that the answer may be more encouraging than many people realise. While nutrition and lifestyle cannot completely eliminate the risk of fibroids—and they are certainly not cures—they are increasingly recognised as important factors that may influence how fibroids develop, how quickly they grow, and how severe their symptoms become. This emerging evidence offers women, healthcare professionals, and policymakers an opportunity to shift part of the conversation from treatment alone to prevention and early intervention.A Silent Burden Affecting MillionsUterine fibroids, medically known as leiomyomas, are non-cancerous growths that develop within or around the muscular wall of the uterus. Although they are benign, their impact on women’s health can be profound. Scientific studies estimate that between 70 and 80 percent of women will develop uterine fibroids during their reproductive years, making them the most common non-cancerous tumour affecting women worldwide. Many women never develop symptoms, but for countless others, fibroids become a source of chronic pain, heavy menstrual bleeding, anaemia, recurrent miscarriages, infertility, pregnancy complications, and emotional distress. In many parts of Nigeria, these symptoms are often accepted as a normal part of womanhood. A teenage girl who experiences extremely heavy menstrual bleeding may simply be told that she “takes after her mother.” A newly married woman who struggles to conceive may face blame from family members before anyone considers investigating a possible fibroid. Women suffering persistent pelvic discomfort frequently self-medicate or seek traditional remedies long before consulting a qualified healthcare provider. These delays often mean that fibroids continue growing unnoticed until they significantly affect quality of life. Beyond the physical symptoms lies another burden that receives far less attention—the emotional and financial cost. Women living with fibroids may repeatedly miss work because of severe menstrual bleeding or debilitating pain. Others spend years moving from one hospital to another searching for affordable treatment. Families often shoulder enormous healthcare expenses while coping with anxiety surrounding fertility and future pregnancies. Although much of the available economic research comes from the United States, where fibroids are estimated to cost more than 34 billion dollars annually in healthcare expenses and lost productivity, the financial impact in countries like Nigeria may be even more devastating because most healthcare costs are paid directly by patients and their families.Why Black Women Face Greater RiskOne of the most important—and perhaps least understood—findings from recent scientific research is that uterine fibroids do not affect all women equally. Studies consistently show that Black women develop fibroids more frequently, at younger ages, and often experience larger tumours and more severe symptoms than women from many other racial groups. They are also more likely to require surgical treatment during their reproductive years. Scientists believe this disparity results from a complex interaction of genetics, hormones, environmental exposures, vitamin D deficiency, healthcare access, and social determinants of health rather than any single cause. For Nigeria, these findings carry enormous significance. With one of Africa’s largest populations of women of reproductive age, Nigeria may already bear a substantial share of the global burden of uterine fibroids. Yet awareness remains relatively low, preventive education is limited, and many women first learn about fibroids only after symptoms become severe enough to require medical intervention. This reality presents an opportunity for public health leaders. Instead of focusing almost exclusively on surgery after fibroids have developed, greater attention can be given to helping women understand the lifestyle and nutritional factors that research suggests may influence risk before serious complications occur. Importantly, this approach does not imply that women are responsible for causing fibroids. Many risk factors—including age, genetics, and hormonal influences—cannot be changed. However, growing scientific evidence indicates that several lifestyle behaviours are modifiable and may contribute to reducing risk or slowing disease progression.Changing the Conversation from Treatment to PreventionFor decades, medical management of fibroids has centred largely on monitoring tumour growth until symptoms become severe enough to justify medication or surgery. While these treatments remain essential, they do little to address the underlying factors that may contribute to fibroid development. Today, researchers around the world are increasingly exploring a different question: What if prevention began long before surgery became necessary? Emerging evidence suggests that nutrition, vitamin D status, body weight, physical activity, stress management, and environmental exposures may all play meaningful roles in fibroid development. Although researchers continue to study these relationships, the findings already point toward an important public health message: healthy lifestyle choices may not only improve overall wellbeing but could also become valuable tools in reducing the burden of uterine fibroids. For Nigerian women, this shift in thinking could transform how fibroids are discussed—not simply as a condition to be treated after diagnosis, but as a women’s health issue that deserves earlier education, preventive action, and greater national attention. • Obi, MPH, is a public health researcher and graduate of Monroe University, New York. Her work focuses on women’s health, epidemiology, nutrition, disease prevention, and health equity, particularly in African populations. The post Beyond Surgery: Can nutrition and lifestyle help prevent Uterine Fibroids? appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: ‘I regret snatching my friend’s husband’ — Reader
items.description: By Bunmi Sofola A Reader wrote: I have followed your columns way back from your Punch days when I was in the university. Most of the times, your articles are so down-to-earth they speak to me – as if you are writing about me. In one of the editions of Sunday Vanguard a few months back, you wrote about why second marriages might not work. I am a living example of that. I’d been married for over 12 years with three children when I changed jobs for a challenging management post in a bank. The salary almost doubled what I earned and I quickly made friends with a colleague who was about the same age. Her name is Tina and it was inevitable that both families met. “We attended each other’s functions and Francis, Tina’s husband, was a particularly friendly chap. Tina had regaled me with stories of his affairs but I saw the reason why women found him attractive – he was dishy! When Tina travelled abroad on a course and Francis came to the office, I wondered what he wanted. Thinking he needed help with his bank account, I went to him. But he said he just dropped by because he was lonely and missed Tina so much. He also missed her home-cooking. I was touched and promised to drop some packaged meals at his place. He was to put them in the freezer and help himself whenever he felt hungry. “True to my word, I dropped the meals at the house of a very eager Francis. He offered to pay for them, but I refused. He insisted I stayed for a drink. To be frank with you, Francis had always intrigued me. I mean, he must have something special for all those women to be panting after him. So, when he made a pass at me, I didn’t resist. Like a lamb to the slaughter, I let him lead me to his matrimonial bed. I wasn’t disappointed – Francis really knew how to bonk! Why else was I risking my marriage for this? He made my head spin with his love-making, transporting me to places I never imagined possible. “That was how our affair started. So though Tina and I worked together, I parcelled off the guilty I felt at helping myself to her husband. I knew we were playing with fire – both of us were married with children and Tina, my friend, was the one who’d introduced me to her husband. That shows the extent of her trust and complacency in her marriage. Seun, my husband and I had since lost the magic of our early years. Even then, he wasn’t as hot as Francis was. Comparing Seun to Francis was like comparing a Christmas sparkler to a rocket! My head had already been turned by Francis’ sizzling, scorching ways. So the affair continued for about a year before the bubble burst. I was returning from another illicit date with Francis when my husband was waiting for me with a disgusted look on his face. “Tina just rang”, he spat. “She saw you with her husband coming out of an hotel. She said she’d become suspicious of her husband yet again and had followed him only to see both of you together. “All the glow of our love-making drained out of me. “We are just friends having a meal together …” I panicked. Seun warned I shouldn’t insult his intelligence. Instead, I should be thinking of what to tell my friend when I faced her in the office the next day. As for this sham of marriage, Seun told me it was now dust. He couldn’t cope with the thought that his wife had been having a torrid affair with a supposed family friend for months. What I had was not a fling, he told me nastily, it was a relationship and I was now free to pursue my passion. “The hardest part was facing Tina in the office. She made a scene and all eyes were on me as if I’d committed a crime. Our head of department invited us both to his office when he heard the commotion, and to be fair to him, he didn’t pass judgement. All he said was that we’d both fouled up the office atmosphere and one of us would have to be transferred to another branch. I quickly offered to go. I felt really awful at first. But Francis was really sorry for breaking up my marriage and quickly found me a flat, which I moved into with two of my children. “My eldest, a boy, decided to stay with his father. So that was how Francis and I became a reluctant couple, Tina stayed put in her matrimonial home – she’s used to her husband’s philandering. Whatever sadness I felt at the death of my marriage was quickly erased by Francis’ love-making. Fate put on its final seal when I discovered I was pregnant. It wasn’t planned and I was really angry with myself. Francis, on the other hand was delighted and before the baby was due, insisted on a traditional marriage. Seun had already instituted a divorce anyway and I would be a fool to contest it with a full-blown pregnancy! “I couldn’t socialize because most of our friends were aware of what happened and they weren’t sympathetic – especially the married ones. They openly disapproved of it. The birth of our son didn’t help much. I couldn’t find a convenient house help and when Francis visited, I wasn’t the temptress he was used to. But as soon as the boy was a toddler, we were back to a semblance of romance. Only as the years rolled by, I still felt like the other woman – but without the excitement and sparks. Tina still lived with her husband and when Francis took our son to visit his four other kids, my blood boiled because Tina would be there probably with her disapproving look. “Seven years after my husband threw me out, passion with Francis now meant screaming arguments, not frenzied love-making. He’d since had a couple of affairs I was aware of and we kept falling out, then falling into each other’s arms. Only the making up because less and less. Seun had already remarried though he had a very good rapport with two of our children that lived with me. I’d made my bed, building it on deceit. Was lying in it now my just desert? It was then I started having panic attacks and palpitations. My doctor said it was stress-related. My illicit love life was affecting my health. “Now that my complaints had become second nature, I saw Francis less and less. He’d bought us a flat in his son’s name and wasn’t really keen on sex. When I discovered he’d started yet another affair, it didn’t even bother me until I learnt that she was pregnant. Francis had always believed I had affairs from time to time. If I could do it when I was properly married, what stopped me from doing it now that I was a quasi wife? I couldn’t blame him really – betraying my ex-husband’s trust for a fling with him has damaged my credibility. “As he spent more and more time with his younger wife, I saw very little of him. Tina is still married to him and he’s set up home with his younger lover. These days, on the few occasions I see Tina at official functions, she was gloat at me with a wry smile. A husband snatcher who’d been given a dose of her medicine. Thank goodness, I still have my job – it’s a stabilising force in a world of passion gone wrong …” Your faithful reader. The post ‘I regret snatching my friend’s husband’ — Reader appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Election rigging: Universities should reply Obi, by Tonnie Iredia
items.description: A scathing recent remark by the presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress NDC, Mr. Peter Obi that Nigerian professors now help illiterates to rig elections in the country must have disconcerted many citizens. It is certainly a remark which keeps Nigeria quite low in the comity of nations more so as it shows the irony of the most read serving the unethical needs of the least read. It is however doubtful if professors go all out to look for only illiterates to offer such patronizing service to. The truth of the matter is that what is pushing the affected professors is greed and not the status of the recipients of the service. It is clear that in a bid to make additional money for themselves, the professors are working for whoever can pay for the service whether such ‘masters’ are illiterates or not. They are indeed working for the highest bidder; meaning they can gain from more than one customer. Such commercialists are not in the least bothered about the implications of their actions especially the effect the posture has for their country. What is in it for me, as the saying goes is what motivates the conduct which seems to suggest that it is a way of life that will persist no matter who is condemning it. In truth, Peter Obi was not the first to highlight the condescending act. Earlier in the year, a former Vice-Chancellor of the Alex Ekwueme Federal University, Ndufu-Alike, Professor Chinedum Nwajiuba called for a halt to the practice of engaging Nigerian professors for election duties. He made the call in a lecture he delivered last February as part of programmes marking the end of the administration of the Vice-Chancellor of the Michael Okpara University of Agriculture Umudike, Professor Maduebibisi Ofo Iwe. Nwajiuba, condemned the apparent eagerness of high-ranking academics to serve as electoral officials, saying that it has considerably diminished their status. He cited some instances when highly regarded academics ended up messing their hard-earned images while performing election duties for INEC and getting caught enmeshed in political intrigues. According to the former VC, “we saw in a governorship election in 2019, a Vice-Chancelor who obtained a first class in mathematics, with a PhD in mathematics and who became a professor of mathematics, but unable to correctly work out, two-thirds of 27 local government areas of a state…. at a review of the 2019 elections, in a meeting held at Radisson Blue Hotel Ikeja, with foreign partners present, it was truly embarrassing.” The poor showing at Ikeja could not have been poorer than what the entire nation saw with many professors who served as returning officers finding it difficult to read out figures they wrote by themselves as votes scored by different candidates in an election. In another clime, the Independent National Electoral Commission INEC would have put a halt to the indiscriminate use of Vice-Chancellors of federal universities as returning officers for general elections. Top-ranking lecturers on their part would not have needed any call for them to see why they should reject such assignments. But we can conclusively say that our university chieftains are not likely to listen to Nwajiuba or other analysts. After all, their umbrella body, the Academic Staff Union of Universities ASUU had earlier similarly publicised the same admonition but in vain. It would be recalled that ASUU itself stopped the policy of participating or deploying members as a union to election duties after finding the general election structure flawed. It ruled that any set of university lecturers serving as returning or collation officers for INEC were ‘doing so on their own accord rather than as an institutional representative of ASUU.’ This sounds funny because ASUU is saying that if a lecturer misbehaves at a public function, it will have no negative effect on ASUU, it is only the lecturer that would be disgraced. It would appear that our universities as institutions have the same opinion and as such do not bother about the shame that debased lecturers bring back from election duties. If so, how are such lecturers able to participate in determining students who excelled in knowledge and character? When Professor Attahiru Jega became the chairman of INEC, he introduced the policy of deploying university lecturers as returning officers to boost the credibility of the electoral body. The policy, assumed that highly educated individuals would possess the moral integrity to resist political manipulation. Those of us who knew that the assumption was unduly simplistic wondered how such a conclusion was easily arrived at. Were all the abuses in our universities especially examination malpractices done by ghosts, farmers and other persons outside the universities? Well, within one election cycle, we were proved right. Jega himself publicly lamented that certain academics compromised their positions by colluding with politicians to manipulate electoral outcomes. Initially, the nation was misled into believing that the high-ranking academics only announced what was sent to them until we got to the peak in which courts convicted professors for manufacturing figures different from those sent to them from collation centres. In other words, there were professors who personally controlled the manipulation. Although many of them were helped out of the hook, the few that were convicted established beyond reasonable doubt that to be a professor does not create any immunity around the holder which stops him from being a bad influence on society. For those who had the misfortune of serving in locations supervised by activists like Mike Igini, it was just impossible to get out of trouble. They were duly prosecuted, convicted and sent to jail rubbishing all their academic laurels. In the Southeast, a human rights Organization, under the name, International Society for Civil Liberties and Rule of Law (Intersociety) commissioned an independent investigation which revealed scores of Vice-Chancellors/Professors and others who were behind the reported rigging of the 2023 Polls in the region. The group named citizens that helped to rig the general elections of 2023. At the same time, the group spent ample time eulogising some people in the academic community who refused to be part of fake results. Among them were: Prof. Nnenna Oti, Vice Chancellor of Federal University of Science and Technology FUTO, Owerri, Prof. Charles Esimone, VC-Nnamdi Azikiwe University, UNIZIK, Awka, Prof Maduebibisi Iwe, VC- Federal University of Agriculture, Umudike, Abia state, and Prof. Uzochukwu, Resident Electoral Commissioner REC for Abia state. The point to be made is that every profession or group has its bad eggs. It is therefore wrong to condemn a group because of such a segment, no matter the size. Today, many people are unsettled by many judicial decisions especially those that are usually overturned by the higher courts. Despite such infamous judgments greatly increasing by the day and causing severe concerns to some people, we still have to recognize that not everyone in the sector has become mad. There are still a few who continue to give of their best. What this suggests is that we cannot keep to the idea of getting university officials to help solve our election debacle which has been greatly compounded by them. To do so is to continue to do the same thing while expecting a different result. The blind can now see that the old idea that the academic community is the model which the rest of society should emulate is stale. We need to design better modalities for identifying people of integrity in our society that can be trusted to take society away from certain ills. Painfully, the universities have chosen to be silent as if that can redeem the damaged image foisted on them by some of their greedy and irrational members. Gone were the days when our universities stood in unison against societal ills – unacceptable decisions affecting not the universities particularly but the nation in general. For instance, it was the critical segments of our universities that stopped the obnoxious Anglo-Nigeria Defence Pact of 1961. Peter Obi and other critics who have openly condemned the new posture of our universities for being part of the unacceptable conduct of falsifying election results must get a reply. The academia must be active in bringing the discredit to an end because it was super active in elevating it to its current high degree. Our universities will keep a dented image if they continue to pretend that what lecturers are known for now in election is caused by the individual lecturers and not their institutions. There is no gain in playing the ostrich. The post Election rigging: Universities should reply Obi, by Tonnie Iredia appeared first on Vanguard News .
